front.title: Multi-Tenant Profile for JOSE Composite Post-Quantum Signatures

abstract.t: This document defines a multi-tenant profile for JOSE composite post-quantum signatures. The profile specifies how a JOSE issuer operating in a multi-tenant environment (a SaaS platform signing tokens on behalf of multiple tenants) constructs, identifies, and validates composite signatures combining classical and post-quantum algorithms, with per-tenant key isolation and algorithm policy enforcement.

The profile addresses the operational requirements of multi-tenant deployment: tenant-bound key derivation, deterministic composite algorithm identification in the JWS header, and validation rules that prevent cross-tenant signature confusion during the post-quantum transition.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: JOSE defines the JSON Web Signature structure used to protect JWTs and other JSON content. Composite post-quantum signatures, combining a classical algorithm (e.g., ECDSA P-256) with a post-quantum algorithm (e.g., ML-DSA ), provide a transition path: they remain secure if either component remains unbroken. Draft specifications for composite JOSE signatures define the algorithm identifiers and the two-layer or combined signing structure.

In a multi-tenant SaaS environment, a single platform issues signed tokens on behalf of many tenants. Each tenant may have distinct key material, distinct algorithm policy, and distinct trust expectations. Naive application of composite signatures in this setting risks cross-tenant confusion: a validator might accept a token signed under tenant A's key as if it were tenant B's, or might apply the wrong algorithm policy to a token. This profile specifies the binding between a composite signature and its tenant context to eliminate these risks.

section.name: Motivation
section.t: Multi-tenant token issuance is common in SaaS platforms, identity providers, and API gateways. As these platforms adopt post-quantum signatures, they must do so without weakening the tenant isolation guarantees that classical deployments provide. A dedicated profile ensures that composite signature adoption does not introduce new cross-tenant attack surfaces.

section.name: Conventions and Definitions
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals as shown here.

section.name: Header Requirements
section.t: A JWS protected header under this profile MUST include the following header parameters in addition to those required by :

dl.dd: A stable, opaque identifier for the tenant on whose behalf the token is signed. Validators MUST bind the tenant identifier to the expected tenant context before accepting the signature.
The key identifier. Under this profile, kid MUST be unique within a tenant's key set; validators MUST NOT treat kid as globally unique. Key resolution MUST be scoped by tenant first, then kid.
The composite algorithm identifier (e.g., ES256P-ML-DSA-65). The header MUST NOT list the component algorithms separately; the composite identifier is authoritative.

section.t: The tenant parameter is the linchpin of multi-tenant isolation. A validator that ignores tenant and resolves kid globally risks accepting a token from the wrong tenant.

section.name: Key Resolution
section.t: Key resolution under this profile is a two-step process:

ol.li: Resolve the tenant's key set using the tenant header parameter. The tenant-to-key-set mapping MUST be established out of band and MUST be authenticated.
Within the tenant's key set, resolve the kid to a specific composite public key. If kid is absent or does not match a key in the resolved tenant key set, validation MUST fail.

section.t: This two-step resolution prevents the global-kid collision attack: an attacker who controls tenant A cannot craft a token with a kid matching tenant B's key, because resolution is scoped to the declared tenant first.

section.name: Validation Rules
section.t: A validator implementing this profile MUST:

li.t: Reject any JWS whose header omits tenant.
Reject any JWS whose tenant does not identify a known tenant in the validator's configuration.
Reject any JWS whose alg is not an approved composite algorithm per the tenant's configured algorithm policy.
Verify both component signatures of the composite; failure of either component MUST cause overall validation failure.
Reject any JWS whose tenant header conflicts with tenant context established elsewhere in the token (e.g., a iss claim that implies a different tenant).

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: The primary threat addressed by this profile is cross-tenant signature confusion, in which a token signed under one tenant's key is accepted as if signed under another's. The two-step key resolution and the mandatory tenant header parameter prevent this, provided validators implement the resolution order correctly. A validator that resolves kid before tenant reintroduces the vulnerability.

Composite signatures are only as strong as their combiner. This profile mandates verification of both components but does not redefine combiner semantics; it relies on the composite algorithm specification's combiner. Implementations MUST use the combiner defined by the referenced composite algorithm, not a custom construction.

Per-tenant key isolation requires that the platform's key management does not permit one tenant's signing operation to access another tenant's key material. This is an operational requirement outside the scope of the JOSE header but is a precondition for the security of this profile.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document has no IANA actions. The tenant header parameter is a private header parameter under the JOSE registry's private-use space. A future revision may request registration of tenant in the JSON Web Signature and Encryption Header Parameters registry if standardization is desired.
